summary: The Network Information Center announces the weekdays and hours its online system would be available to network users, starting October 4, 1971. Some periods are set aside for development and may be irregular. It also explains what users see after a Telnet connection is made.

eli5.summary: A shop posting its opening hours. It says when the information computer is open to visitors, and that sometimes it might ask you to leave early.

subtitle: When the first network information service opens for business.

tldr.problem: The ARPANET community needs a way to find information about the network and available resources, but has no shared service yet.
tldr.mechanism: The Network Information Center announces it will operate an online system accessible via Telnet, with regular hours starting October 4, 1971, plus some irregular availability for system development.
tldr.outcome: Users can connect at published times to retrieve network information and resource documentation.

today: RFC 223 documents the operational schedule and access procedures for one of the first centralized information services on the ARPANET. It is a historical snapshot of early network administration and user support practices.

sections.title: Network Information Center Hours
sections.content:
RFC 223 announces the operating schedule for the Network Information Center (NIC), which will provide service to ARPANET users on a regular basis Monday through Friday starting October 4, 1971. Times are given in Pacific Daylight or Pacific Standard Time.

The daily schedule is: 0500 to 1200 (except Tuesdays 0800 to 1200), 1200 to 1300 unavailable, 1300 to 1800 available, and 1800 to 2200 available on an irregular basis for system development. The system is also available irregularly on weekends.
sections.eli5: The information office opens in the early morning until noon, closes for lunch, reopens in the afternoon, and may work late for repairs.

sections.title: Access via Telnet
sections.content:
Users access the NIC system by establishing a Telnet connection. When a user's Telnet connection is established, the system herald is printed, followed by a brief message to network users containing items of particular interest.

To log in, users provide their site identifier as the username, use the password ARPA, and provide an account number consisting of the site identifier followed by the user's last name. For example, connecting as ucla-postel logs in John Postel from UCLA.
sections.eli5: You connect to the computer, it says hello and shows you any news, then you type your site name, the password, and your name to sign in.

sections.title: Support and Contact Information
sections.content:
The RFC lists contact persons for different kinds of problems. Dick Watson handles administrative issues. John Melvin addresses NCP or Telnet problems. Marily Auerbach and Dirk van Nouhuys handle TNLS problems. If NIC personnel do not answer directly, an answering service takes messages and NIC staff responds each morning.

The document includes a table of site identifiers, names, and phone numbers for network sites, allowing users to determine how to reach each institution. Most sites are reachable via Enterprise or Zenith numbers through operators, though some support dial-direct access.
sections.eli5: If you have trouble connecting, you can call different people depending on what is wrong, and they will help you or call back the next day.
